title: Professional Scrum Master II (PSM II)
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the Scrum Guide 2020 and Scrum.org PSM II subject areas (advanced Scrum application). Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.stem: A Scrum Master notices that the Developers consistently wait for direction from the Product Owner before starting any task on the Sprint Backlog. Which action best serves the Scrum Master's accountability?
options: Coach the Developers so they learn to self-manage their work within the Sprint
Ask the Product Owner to prepare a detailed task list for the Developers
Assign tasks personally each morning at the Daily Scrum
Escalate the Developers' dependency to the engineering manager
items.explanation: The Scrum Master coaches the Scrum Team toward self-management. Handing out tasks, whether by the Product Owner or the Scrum Master, preserves the dependency, and escalating to a manager treats a coaching opportunity as a performance problem.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Scrum Mastery

items.stem: At the Sprint Review the Developers only demonstrate completed features and never discuss adapting the Product Backlog. How should the Scrum Master respond?
options: Ask the Product Owner to present the backlog alone next time
Remind the team that the Sprint Review is a working session to inspect the Increment and adapt the Product Backlog
Cancel the Sprint Review because it adds no value to the stakeholders
Replace the Sprint Review with a formal sign-off meeting
items.explanation: The Sprint Review exists so the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the Increment and adapt the Product Backlog. Treating it as a demo or replacing it with sign-off removes the empirical inspection and adaptation the event is meant to create.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Scrum Mastery

items.stem: The Scrum Master observes that the Definition of Done has been quietly weakened so that work can be called complete sooner. What is the best first action?
options: Accept it because the team owns its own Definition of Done
Restore the previous Definition of Done unilaterally
Raise the observation with the Scrum Team and explore why the quality standard changed
Report the Developers to the Product Owner for lowering quality
items.explanation: A weakened Definition of Done threatens transparency, so the Scrum Master surfaces the issue with the team and coaches them to understand the consequences. Punishing the team or unilaterally overwriting their agreement undermines self-management and treats the symptom rather than the cause.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Scrum Mastery

items.stem: Under schedule pressure the Developers propose skipping the Sprint Retrospective for this Sprint. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: Agree to skip it once because the schedule is at risk
Hold the Retrospective alone and send the team the notes
Replace the Retrospective with a written survey
Coach the team on the value of the Retrospective and help them keep the event within the timebox
items.explanation: The Retrospective is the inspect-and-adapt event for the team's way of working, so the Scrum Master protects it and helps the team fit it into a shorter timebox rather than dropping it. Skipping, running it without the team, or substituting a survey all remove the team's opportunity to improve.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Scrum Mastery

items.stem: The Developers finish work each Sprint, but the Increment is never integrated and cannot be released. Which action best reflects the Scrum Master's role?
options: Coach the team to meet the Definition of Done so that an integrated, usable Increment exists at the end of the Sprint
Ask the Product Owner to accept partially integrated work
Add a release manager to integrate the work after each Sprint
Move integration into a hardening Sprint later in the quarter
items.explanation: The Definition of Done exists so that the Increment is usable and potentially releasable. A hardening Sprint or a separate integrator hides the problem rather than fixing it, and accepting partial integration erases transparency about real progress.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Scrum Mastery

items.stem: Mid-Sprint the Developers realise the Sprint Goal has become obsolete because of new market information. Who should decide how to respond?
options: The Developers should silently continue toward the original goal
The Scrum Team should inspect the situation and decide with the Product Owner whether to change the Sprint Goal
The Scrum Master should decide and instruct the Developers
The engineering manager should approve any change to the Sprint Goal
items.explanation: The Sprint Goal is owned by the Scrum Team and can be adjusted through conversation with the Product Owner as new information arrives. Unilateral decisions by the Scrum Master or a manager, or silently continuing against obsolete information, all break empiricism.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Scrum Mastery

items.stem: A new Developer asks the Scrum Master to choose between two competing technical designs. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Refer the decision to the Product Owner
Tell the Developer to escalate the choice to the architect
Coach the Developer to evaluate the options with the team so the team makes the decision
Choose the design that seems safest to keep the Sprint on track
items.explanation: Technical decisions belong with the people doing the work, and the Scrum Master serves by coaching rather than deciding. Making the call, pushing it to the Product Owner, or escalating to an architect keeps authority away from the Developers and weakens self-management.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Scrum Mastery

items.stem: Three Scrum Teams build one product but maintain three separate Product Backlogs with conflicting priorities. What should the Scrum Master do first?
options: Let each team optimise its own backlog independently
Ask each team to nominate a backlog owner and sync weekly
Merge the three teams into one large team immediately
Help the organisation adopt a single Product Backlog owned by one Product Owner to improve transparency and flow
items.explanation: A single product has one Product Backlog and one Product Owner so that priorities are coherent and empiricism works across the product. Parallel backlogs create conflicting priorities, a committee of owners still fragments accountability, and forcing an immediate merge ignores the wider system.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Scrum Mastery

items.stem: The Daily Scrum has turned into a status report where each Developer reports to a manager who attends. Which action best fits the Scrum Master's accountability?
options: Coach the team to refocus the Daily Scrum on inspecting progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapting the plan
Ask the manager to stop attending without any further discussion
Move the Daily Scrum to a private channel to avoid the manager
Accept the format because it keeps management informed
items.explanation: The Daily Scrum is for the Developers to inspect progress and adapt their plan toward the Sprint Goal. Simply excluding the manager or hiding the event does not teach the intended purpose, and accepting a status-report format reinforces the behaviour.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Scrum Mastery

items.stem: A Scrum Team claims to be agile but its Product Owner gives the Developers a complete specification and expects no changes during the Sprint. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: Document the conflict and take no action because the team is still delivering
Coach the Scrum Team and its stakeholders on empiricism and the value of learning within a Sprint
Tell the Developers to follow the specification exactly
Ask the Product Owner to leave the team permanently
items.explanation: The Scrum Master coaches the wider environment toward empiricism and collaboration. Enforcing a fixed specification, removing the Product Owner, or ignoring the mismatch all leave the underlying way of working unchanged.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Scrum Mastery

items.stem: During a Sprint Retrospective two Developers exchange sharp personal criticism and the room goes quiet. As facilitator what should the Scrum Master do?
options: Side with the more experienced Developer to restore order
Ignore the exchange and continue with the planned agenda
Acknowledge the tension, restate the ground rules, and guide the group back to the issues rather than the people
End the Retrospective and reschedule it for a calmer day
items.explanation: A facilitator protects the purpose and safety of the session by naming the tension and refocusing on issues rather than people. Ending the event avoids the conflict, taking sides damages safety, and ignoring it lets the discussion deteriorate.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Facilitation and Coaching

items.stem: A Product Owner asks the Scrum Master to direct the Developers on what to build next because the team is not moving fast enough. How should the Scrum Master respond?
options: Start assigning tasks to the Developers as requested
Tell the Product Owner to raise a ticket for each request
Escalate the Product Owner to the management team
Explain that the Product Owner orders the Product Backlog and the Developers decide how to deliver it, then help improve flow
items.explanation: The Product Owner owns ordering the Product Backlog while the Developers own how the work is done. Directing the Developers blurs accountability, a ticketing process does not address flow, and escalating the Product Owner damages the partnership the Scrum Master should build.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Facilitation and Coaching

items.stem: The Product Owner is overwhelmed and asks the Scrum Master to order the Product Backlog on their behalf. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Coach the Product Owner on ordering techniques and help them make the decisions themselves
Order the backlog quickly and hand it back to the Product Owner
Ask the Developers to order the backlog together
Leave the backlog unordered until the Product Owner finds time
items.explanation: Accountability for ordering the Product Backlog stays with the Product Owner, so the Scrum Master teaches techniques rather than taking it over. Doing it for them, delegating it to the Developers, or leaving it unordered all weaken the Product Owner's accountability.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Facilitation and Coaching

items.stem: In a Retrospective the team offers only safe, surface-level observations and avoids the difficult topics. Which facilitation approach is best?
options: Ask the manager to identify the real problems for the team
Use structured techniques and targeted questions to surface issues while maintaining psychological safety
Publicly challenge the quietest team member to speak up
Cancel future Retrospectives since the team clearly does not want them
items.explanation: Skilled facilitation uses structure and open questions to make it safer to raise hard issues. Singling out a quiet member, cancelling the event, or asking a manager to diagnose problems all reduce the safety and ownership the Retrospective depends on.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Facilitation and Coaching

items.stem: A Developer repeatedly asks the Scrum Master for the right answer to every problem instead of thinking it through. Which coaching stance is most appropriate?
options: Stop responding to the Developer's questions entirely
Reassign the Developer's problems to another team member
Ask reflective questions that help the Developer reason about the problem and reach their own answer
Give the answer each time so the Developer is not delayed
items.explanation: Coaching builds capability through reflection and open questions. Answering every time creates dependency, ignoring the person is not coaching, and moving the problems to someone else avoids the developmental need the developer is showing.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Facilitation and Coaching

items.stem: Two Developers disagree strongly and repeatedly about coding standards, and the disagreement is spreading to the whole team. What should the Scrum Master do first?
options: Impose a coding standard chosen by the most senior Developer
Ask the two Developers to stop talking to each other
Report both Developers to their functional managers
Facilitate a session where the team agrees on shared standards and how to decide future disputes
items.explanation: Facilitating an agreement and a decision process lets the team own the standard and resolve future conflicts. Imposing a standard, silencing the individuals, or escalating to managers removes ownership and leaves the conflict unresolved.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Facilitation and Coaching

items.stem: Several new members join a Scrum Team and openly describe traditional roles such as team lead and tester. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: Coach the whole team on the Scrum accountabilities and help them apply them in practice
Create formal team lead and tester roles to match their expectations
Ignore it because experienced people will adjust on their own
Ask the new members to read the Scrum Guide and report back
items.explanation: The Scrum Master teaches Scrum so the team can apply it, and does so with the whole team in context. Creating legacy roles, passively waiting, or delegating learning to reading without support all slow the change and can entrench old habits.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Facilitation and Coaching

items.stem: Each Retrospective the team lists the same problems and takes no action on them. What is the best next step for the Scrum Master?
options: Decide that the problems are outside the team's control and stop raising them
Help the team choose a small number of improvements and hold themselves accountable for them
Write the action items and assign them to individuals
Reduce the Retrospective to a brief check-in
items.explanation: The Retrospective should end with concrete, owned improvements, so the Scrum Master coaches the team to focus and follow through. The Scrum Master assigning the work, shortening the event, or giving up reverses the intent of inspecting and adapting.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Facilitation and Coaching

items.stem: A stakeholder asks the Scrum Master to present the team's Sprint progress to executives because the team is too busy. How should the Scrum Master approach the request?
options: Refuse and tell the stakeholder to read the Sprint Backlog
Compress the Sprint Review into a private summary for executives only
Help the team and Product Owner share progress transparently and coach stakeholders on how Scrum provides visibility
Accept the task and report on the team's behalf permanently
items.explanation: The Scrum Master serves the organisation by increasing the effectiveness of Scrum and the transparency of the work. Becoming a permanent reporter, refusing outright, or privatising the Sprint Review all reduce transparency instead of improving it.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Facilitation and Coaching

items.stem: An engineering manager asks the Scrum Master to rate each Developer's productivity monthly. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Produce the monthly productivity ratings as requested
Ask the Developers to rate each other instead
Decline to speak with the manager about the topic
Coach the manager on how Scrum teams measure progress and explore what decision the data is meant to support
items.explanation: The Scrum Master coaches the organisation toward complementary practices and useful transparency. Producing individual ratings or peer ratings undermines the team and self-management, and refusing to discuss the need leaves the request unaddressed.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Facilitation and Coaching

items.stem: A Scrum Team is repeatedly blocked by a slow procurement process that sits outside its control. What should the Scrum Master do first?
options: Make the impediment visible to the organisation and work with the relevant people to remove it
Advise the team to plan around the delay
Ask the team to bypass the procurement process privately
Add the impediment to the Retrospective agenda and wait
items.explanation: Removing impediments that the team cannot remove itself is a core accountability of the Scrum Master and requires influencing the wider organisation. Bypassing a control may breach governance, planning around the delay does not remove it, and only noting it lets the problem persist.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Organizational Agility

items.stem: Several Scrum Teams share one product and regularly block one another with cross-team dependencies. Which action best improves organisational agility?
options: Split the product so each team works on unrelated components
Make dependencies visible and coach the teams and management to reduce them through better structure and collaboration
Ask each team to buffer its Sprints with extra contingency work
Assign a coordinator to schedule all cross-team work top-down
items.explanation: Scaling Scrum works best when dependencies are made transparent and the system is changed to reduce them. Buffering hides the problem, a top-down scheduler shifts control away from teams, and cutting the product into unrelated parts can harm the integrated product.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Organizational Agility

items.stem: Management wants to use each team's velocity as the official measure of productivity and compare teams against one another. How should the Scrum Master respond?
options: Provide the velocity comparisons in the monthly report
Stop the teams from tracking any metrics at all
Coach management on what velocity can and cannot indicate and suggest measures of value and outcomes instead
Standardise the teams' estimating so velocity becomes comparable
items.explanation: Velocity is team-specific and cannot be compared across teams, so the Scrum Master educates management and steers toward outcome-focused measures. Forcing comparable estimates or supplying misleading comparisons harms empiricism, and banning all metrics removes useful transparency.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Organizational Agility

items.stem: A recurring impediment is caused by an organisational policy rather than by the team itself. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: Keep helping the team work around the policy each Sprint
Tell the team to accept the policy as fixed
Record the impediment in the Retrospective and move on
Address the systemic cause by engaging decision makers and coaching the organisation to change the policy
items.explanation: The Scrum Master serves the organisation by removing barriers between stakeholders and teams, which means addressing root causes. Repeated workarounds, accepting the policy as fixed, or merely recording it leave the systemic problem in place.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Organizational Agility

items.stem: Middle managers believe that Scrum removes their purpose and quietly resist the change. Which action best supports organisational agility?
options: Engage the managers to understand their concerns and redefine their role so they support the teams
Ask senior leadership to remove the resisting managers
Work around the managers and hope the resistance fades
Pause the Scrum adoption until the managers retire
items.explanation: Sustainable change requires engaging people affected by it and helping them find a constructive role. Removing managers, avoiding them, or waiting them out all create conflict and stall the organisational change the Scrum Master should nurture.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Organizational Agility

items.stem: Leaders want a single dashboard that reports progress across many teams to steer the work weekly. What should the Scrum Master advise?
options: Allow the dashboard but let it override each team's Sprint Goals
Focus the dashboard on outcomes and trends and coach leaders to inspect and adapt rather than direct the teams
Build the dashboard from every team's hourly velocity data
Refuse to provide any information to leadership
items.explanation: Leadership alignment comes from transparency about outcomes and shared direction, not from controlling team-level detail. Micro-metric dashboards and overrides undermine self-management, while refusing transparency is unhelpful.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Organizational Agility

items.stem: An organisation adopts Scrum events but keeps quarterly phase gates with heavy documentation before any release. How should the Scrum Master proceed?
options: Accept the phase gates as non-negotiable and focus only on team delivery
Add more Scrum events to counterbalance the documentation
Make the mismatch visible and coach leaders and teams toward a way of working that supports frequent delivery
Force the teams to skip the phase gates without leadership agreement
items.explanation: Organisational agility depends on aligning structure and governance with empiricism, which the Scrum Master influences through transparency and coaching. Unilateral rule-breaking, passive acceptance, or adding events do not change the underlying system.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Organizational Agility

items.stem: A team consistently misses its Sprint Goal, and the Scrum Master notices that the underlying cause is an enterprise testing bottleneck shared by many teams. What is the best action?
options: Coach the single team harder on estimating its Sprints
Advise the team to lower its Sprint Goals until it stops missing them
Conclude that the team simply lacks discipline
Raise the systemic bottleneck with the organisation and work across teams to remove it
items.explanation: When the cause lies outside one team, the Scrum Master addresses the system rather than blaming the team. Pushing harder on estimates, lowering goals, or attributing the problem to discipline all misdiagnose a shared constraint.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Organizational Agility

items.stem: Stakeholders judge the product only by the number of features delivered each Sprint, ignoring whether those features create value. How should the Scrum Master respond?
options: Coach stakeholders toward outcome-based thinking and help them see the difference between output and value
Instruct the team to deliver more features regardless of value
Remove all feature-related reporting to stop the discussion
Agree that more features always means more success
items.explanation: The Scrum Master helps the organisation focus on value and outcomes rather than raw output. Chasing feature counts or validating the output mindset harms the product, and hiding reporting removes transparency instead of improving understanding.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Organizational Agility

items.stem: Multiple Scrum Teams must integrate their work every Sprint but each team uses a different Definition of Done. What should the Scrum Master do first?
options: Delay integration until a later hardening phase
Facilitate the teams and Product Owner to agree a shared Definition of Done that supports an integrated Increment
Let each team keep its own Definition of Done with no coordination
Ask management to impose one Definition of Done by policy
items.explanation: For multiple teams building one product, a shared Definition of Done is needed so the combined Increment is usable. Uncoordinated definitions break integration transparency, imposed policy removes team ownership, and delaying integration hides quality problems.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSM II subject areas - Organizational Agility
